title: Comparative advantage
bridge: Trade lets two economies both gain whenever their opportunity costs differ. Where the price lands between those costs, and so who gets the gains, is set by how big each economy is.
blurb: Two economies can both gain from trade at any price between their opportunity costs, but nobody gets to pick the price. An economy that's better at everything, trading with a partner its own size, can come away with nothing at all.

title: Economic rent
bridge: Comparative advantage took each economy's techniques as given. Economic rent asks where a better technique comes from, and follows the reward a firm earns for being different until competition takes it away and spreads the idea.
blurb: Seven technologies can do the same job, and the rectangle test from first courses leaves a sensible middle option standing that isn't the cheapest at any price. Along the way we meet economic rent, and see why the competition that removes it is also what spreads a new idea.

title: Supply and demand
bridge: Economic rent followed one firm's margin as competition closed it. Supply and demand steps up to the whole market, and shows that a line through its prices and quantities is a mix of the two curves rather than the demand curve.
blurb: A line through a market's prices and quantities is a mix of demand and supply, not the demand curve. The R² that says how well the line fits also says how little the data can tell us about demand.

title: Elasticity
bridge: Supply and demand took the slopes of the curves as given. Elasticity looks at how strongly quantity responds to price, and finds that the answer is a ratio of two lengths that each point cuts from its own tangent.
blurb: Elasticity is a ratio of two lengths that each point on a demand curve cuts from its own tangent. The picture works on any smooth curve, and it shows what the usual two-point formulas assume without saying so.

title: Surplus and efficiency
bridge: Elasticity measured how responsive buyers are along a curve. Surplus and efficiency measures what the gains from trade are worth, and shows that a price ceiling which rations at random loses more than the familiar triangle counts.
blurb: The deadweight loss triangle counts the trades that don't happen. A price ceiling that rations at random adds a second loss, and in a linear market the two come to the size of the cut: cut output by 27% and 27% of the gains from trade are gone.

title: Tax incidence
bridge: Surplus and efficiency measured the gains from trade and what a cut in output loses. Tax incidence puts a tax between the price buyers pay and the price sellers get, and asks who really pays it.
blurb: Collecting a tax from buyers or from sellers doesn't change who ends up paying it, and the elasticity rule for the split is exact only in a straight-line market. At the rate that raises the most money, half the trades are gone and the lost surplus is half the revenue.

title: Cost curves
bridge: Tax incidence took the supply curve as given. Cost curves opens up the firm behind it, and shows that the plant built for an output is run at its own lowest cost per unit at only one output.
blurb: A firm builds the cheapest plant for the output it plans, and yet that plant is almost never run at its own lowest cost per unit. The envelope picture shows why, and why getting the plant a little wrong costs so little.

title: Perfect competition
bridge: Cost curves looked at one firm choosing its plant. Perfect competition lets firms like it into a market one at a time, and shows that because firms come in whole numbers, the long-run supply curve is a sawtooth rather than a flat line.
blurb: Free entry is meant to push the price down to the lowest average cost. Because firms come in whole numbers, entry stops a little short, the firms that are in keep a small profit, and the long-run supply curve becomes a sawtooth.

title: Markup and elasticity
bridge: Perfect competition assumed firms that take the price as given. Markup and elasticity looks at a firm that sets its own price, and shows that the rule linking its markup to the elasticity of demand describes a single point.
blurb: The best markup is one over the elasticity of demand, on every demand curve. But the rule describes a single point, and two curves that agree there can pass on a rise in cost very differently: half of it on one, two and a half times it on the other.

title: Monopolistic competition
bridge: Markup and elasticity looked at one price-setting firm on its own, and perfect competition at many identical ones. Monopolistic competition sits between them, with firms that each sell a slightly different product, and asks how many varieties a market ends up with.
blurb: How many varieties does a market end up with when every firm sells something slightly different? With a finite number of firms, each familiar answer picks up a small correction, and every correction fades as one over the number of firms.

title: Cartels and the prisoner's dilemma
bridge: Monopolistic competition had many firms, each too small to matter much to the others. Cartels and the prisoner's dilemma looks at a market with only a few, where firms try to act together, and shows why the firms that stay out gain the most.
blurb: When a few firms agree to make less, the firms that stay out gain more than the members do. In a simple model of competition, a cartel pays its members only if it takes in almost the whole market, and every member would rather be the firm outside.

title: Tragedy of the commons
bridge: Cartels showed how one firm's output spills over onto its rivals. Tragedy of the commons finds the same kind of spillover on a shared resource, where each user counts the average catch rather than what its extra effort adds, and the resource's rent drains away.
blurb: On a lake anyone can fish, each boat counts the average catch rather than what its extra hours add, so the lake's rent drains away. Most of it is gone once a few boats share the lake, and the second boat does the most damage.

title: Gini and the Lorenz curve
bridge: Tragedy of the commons followed how much value a shared resource loses. Gini and the Lorenz curve closes the microeconomics principles by asking how income is shared out, and what a single number can and can't say about it.
blurb: Two societies can share a Gini while their poorest live very differently, and two credit scorecards can share one while one catches 40% of defaulters in the riskiest tenth of applicants and the other 25.5%. One number can't say where the inequality sits.

title: Measuring GDP
bridge: Gini and the Lorenz curve looked at how income is shared out. Measuring GDP opens the macroeconomics principles by asking how much there is to share, and shows that the minus sign in front of imports is a correction rather than a cost.
blurb: The minus sign in front of imports in C + I + G + X − M is a correction, not a cost. An import changes GDP only through the home production it replaces, and the trade line in a GDP release reads the same whether that's none of it or all of it.

title: Price indices
bridge: Measuring GDP added up a year's production at that year's prices. Price indices asks how to compare prices across years, and finds that a fixed basket overstates the rise in the cost of living by an amount that depends on how readily people switch between goods.
blurb: A fixed basket overstates the cost of living by about half of σ times the variance of the price changes, where σ is how readily people switch between goods. Averaging last year's basket with this year's gets close to the true answer without ever knowing σ.

title: Unemployment flows
bridge: Price indices showed how a single number can hide the switching behind it. Unemployment flows does the same for the unemployment rate, a stock fed by people losing jobs and people finding them, which settles where the two flows balance.
blurb: The unemployment rate settles where job losses and job finding balance, and that depends only on the ratio of the two. So a hiring freeze can nearly double unemployment while layoffs fall, and two towns at 6% can have spells averaging two months in one and eleven in the other.

title: Compound growth
bridge: Unemployment flows looked at how an economy uses the workers it has from month to month. Compound growth turns to the long run, where a one-point gap in growth rates doubles the gap in living standards in about seventy years, and asks what happens when growth is uncertain.
blurb: A one-point gap in growth rates doubles the gap in living standards in about seventy years. But an economy whose growth swings grows more slowly than its average rate, and once growth is uncertain, the typical path falls behind the expected one for ever.

title: Money creation
bridge: Compound growth dealt with real output over decades. Money creation turns to the money that output is bought with, following one loan through three banks' balance sheets to show where deposits come from and what the money multiplier really measures.
blurb: A bank that lends alone loses most of the loan in reserves, which is why bankers say deposits come first. Banks that lend in step lose none, so the system's loans create its deposits, and the money multiplier is a ratio that holds whichever way the causation runs.

title: Constrained choice
bridge: Money creation closed the macroeconomics principles with the banking system as a whole. Constrained choice opens intermediate microeconomics by stepping down to one person's decision, where an indifference curve meets a budget line, and asks what a pay rise does to how much someone chooses to work.
blurb: Many first courses say theory can't tell us whether a pay rise makes people work more or less, and in general that's true. But for the Cobb–Douglas utility they usually draw, the income and substitution effects cancel completely, and hours don't move at any wage.

title: Nash equilibrium
bridge: Constrained choice looked at one person choosing against a fixed budget. Nash equilibrium brings in a second decision maker whose choice depends on ours, and shows what an equilibrium looks like when no cell of the payoff matrix is one.
blurb: In one two-by-two game in eight, checking cells finds no equilibrium, and in those games each player's behaviour is set by the other player's payoffs. So in our model, a bigger fine buys less monitoring and leaves breaches where they were.

title: Bargaining and the surplus
bridge: Nash equilibrium looked at games where both players move at once. Bargaining and the surplus looks at two sides taking turns to make offers, and shows that how impatient each one is picks a single split of the gains.
blurb: Every split on the frontier beats no deal, and the picture can't pick one. Once the two sides take turns making offers, the model settles on a single split, in which your share grows with the other side's impatience, and an outside option counts only once it beats that share.

title: Externalities
bridge: Bargaining and the surplus showed how two sides who can negotiate split the gains from a deal. Externalities brings in a party who isn't at the table, and compares a tax, a quota and a bargain as ways to deal with a cost that nobody prices.
blurb: A tax, a quota and a bargain can bring a polluter down to the same output and move the same money into different pockets. Once the regulator is unsure of the costs, the tax does better when damage is flatter than benefit, and the quota when it's steeper.

title: Efficiency wages
bridge: Externalities assumed the costly action could be seen and measured. Efficiency wages turns to one that can't be, a worker's effort, and shows why a firm might pay more than it has to and leave a queue of people outside.
blurb: When a wage buys effort, the cheapest effort sits where a 1% pay rise buys 1% more effort. That wage comes from the effort curve alone, so a firm hiring one worker or a thousand pays the same, and the queue outside is part of how it works.

title: The order book
bridge: The finance sequence starts where every trade starts, at the queue of orders waiting on an exchange. The order book asks what a market order really pays, and why the shape of that queue matters.
blurb: A market order's average price sits a fixed share of the way from the best quote to the worst price it reaches: half in a flat book, two thirds when depth grows linearly. The shape also decides whether cost grows with size or its square root.

title: Market making
bridge: The order book showed what a market order pays once the quotes are there. Market making asks who sets those quotes, and who ends up paying for the spread between them.
blurb: In Glosten and Milgrom's market the spread moves money from uninformed traders to informed ones, and the market maker breaks even. Halving the informed share halves the spread but makes the price learn four times more slowly, so the uninformed can pay more per piece of news.

title: Short selling and margin
bridge: Market making was about trading with people who know more. Short selling and margin is about trading with borrowed money or borrowed shares, and the broker's rule that comes with them.
blurb: A long bought with half its price borrowed is called after a fall of a third, with two thirds of the stake gone. A short is called after a rise of 15%, and over a year at 30% volatility that happens nearly two times in three.

title: Volatility drag
bridge: Short selling and margin showed a margin account's leverage drifting as prices move. Volatility drag looks at funds that reset their leverage every day instead, and why they drift away from a multiple of the index.
blurb: Over a year, a daily-reset fund's result depends on two numbers, the index's return and how much it moved along the way. A flat year at 20% volatility costs a 3× fund about 11% and a −3× fund about 21%.

title: Index construction
bridge: Volatility drag followed funds that track an index. Index construction asks how the index itself is weighted, and what an equal-weighted index gains by trading back to equal weights.
blurb: An equal-weighted index earns a rebalancing gain by trading back to equal weights, and a cap-weighted one never trades. The gap between them is that gain plus the change in concentration, and when every stock has the same prospects the two nearly cancel.

title: ETF premiums and discounts
bridge: Index construction built the indices that most ETFs track. ETF premiums and discounts asks what keeps an ETF's price close to its holdings, and what a discount to its NAV really means.
blurb: Arbitrage keeps an ETF's price near what its holdings are worth, not near its NAV. When the holdings trade rarely the NAV lags, and in a sell-off a fund can report a deep discount that the NAV closes by catching up.

title: Dividends and buybacks
bridge: The last three articles were about the funds that hold shares. Dividends and buybacks turns to the companies behind them, and the two ways they hand cash back to their shareholders.
blurb: At a fair price a buyback and a dividend of the same size leave shareholders equally well off, though earnings per share rise after one and fall after the other. At the wrong price, a buyback moves wealth between the shareholders who sell and those who stay.

title: The dividend discount model
bridge: Dividends and buybacks showed that how a firm pays out doesn't change what a share is worth. The dividend discount model asks what it is worth in the first place, and why one gap sets both its price and its sensitivity to rates.
blurb: Priced as a growing stream of dividends, a share depends on one gap, the discount rate minus the growth rate. That gap is the dividend yield and the inverse of the duration, so at a 3% gap a one-point rise in rates takes a quarter off the price.

title: Valuation multiples
bridge: The dividend discount model priced a share from its stream of dividends. Valuation multiples reads that price as a ratio to earnings, and asks when growth earns a share a higher one.
blurb: A P/E rises with growth only when the firm reinvests at more than its shareholders need. At a return on equity equal to that 8%, a share is worth 12.5 times earnings however fast it grows, and one P/E fits a whole line of stories about risk and growth.

title: Capital structure
bridge: Valuation multiples took the return shareholders need as given. Capital structure asks what borrowing does to that return, and whether a cheap loan makes a firm any cheaper to fund.
blurb: Borrowing leaves the cost of capital where the assets put it. Shareholders' expected return climbs a straight line only while the loan is safe, and a cost of capital built on the bond's yield rises with borrowing although nothing real has changed.

title: NPV versus IRR
bridge: Capital structure worked out the cost of capital. NPV versus IRR uses it to choose between projects, and asks why the two usual scores can point in opposite directions.
blurb: A project's NPV is its IRR's margin over the cost of capital times the money it keeps tied up. So the IRR compares heights and the NPV compares areas, and a mine with IRRs of 20% and 300% can still lose money at 10%.

title: The Sharpe ratio
bridge: NPV versus IRR scored projects by what they earn. The Sharpe ratio scores a fund's returns against its risk, and asks what happens to it when the fund's prices remember last month.
blurb: Multiplying a monthly Sharpe ratio by the square root of twelve assumes the months don't remember each other. Smoothed prices do, and at a smoothing of 0.6 they double the reported ratio. Lo's correction brings most of it back, but about two months of variance stay hidden in every year.

title: Diversification
bridge: The Sharpe ratio measured one fund's return against its risk. Diversification puts many shares together and asks what holding more of them buys us, in risk and in growth.
blurb: Holding more stocks shrinks risk towards a floor set by how they move together, and ten stocks remove 90% of what can go. It also raises the growth rate by half the variance removed, so over thirty years only one stock in six beats the portfolio.

title: Mean-variance optimisation
bridge: Diversification used equal weights because they were simple. Mean-variance optimisation asks whether the textbook's best weights do better once their inputs have to be estimated from history.
blurb: With estimated average returns, Markowitz's optimiser earns the best Sharpe ratio times the cosine of an angle set by the number of assets and the length of the history. To beat equal weights with ten assets, it needs about 68 years of data.

title: The CAPM and beta
bridge: Mean-variance optimisation chose weights from estimated returns. The CAPM says what those returns should be in equilibrium, a straight line in beta, and this article tests that line against US shares.
blurb: A beta estimated from past returns is noisy, so portfolios sorted on it drift back towards 1, and a line through the sorting betas comes out too flat even where the CAPM holds. Against the betas US portfolios actually had since 1963, the line is still about half as steep.

title: Factor models
bridge: The CAPM left low-beta shares with an alpha. Factor models add more portfolios to the benchmark, and this article traces where an alpha goes each time one is added.
blurb: Adding a factor moves an asset's alpha by minus its loading times the factor's own alpha, so every change can be traced. Value's 4.5% CAPM alpha disappears once investment is priced, the low-beta alpha goes with profitability and investment, and momentum's alpha grows when value joins.

title: The equity premium
bridge: Factor models priced returns against the market. This article asks how well we know the market's own premium, from a century of US returns and from the dividends companies paid.
blurb: A century of US returns puts the equity premium at 8.9% a year, with a 95% band from 4.9% to 12.8%. Monthly data barely narrow it, thirty-year windows range from 4.7% to 14.2%, and since 1950 dividends support about 3 points less than shares returned.

title: The fundamental law of active management
bridge: The equity premium asked how well we know a single average. The fundamental law asks how a manager turns a small, uncertain edge into a steady return by making many bets at once.
blurb: Grinold's law says the information ratio grows with the square root of the number of bets. When a signal's skill swings from month to month, every stock feels it at once, so the ratio stops at the IC divided by the swing, and breadth can lose to conviction.

title: The Kelly criterion
bridge: The fundamental law turned many small bets into a steady return. The Kelly criterion asks how much to stake on each bet so that money grows fastest, and how long that takes to pay off.
blurb: Kelly's bet grows money fastest in the long run, but the long run is measured in units of one over the Sharpe ratio squared. For stocks, Kelly beats half Kelly only 65% of the time after 30 years, and halves our money at some point with probability one half.

title: Efficient markets and the random walk
bridge: The Kelly criterion took the odds of a bet as known. This article asks whether past prices tell us anything about tomorrow's, and what a test that says yes really shows.
blurb: A rule that held the US market after its up days earned 30.5% a year on paper from 1962 to 1986. Stale prices and a bounce between the bid and the ask make efficient markets fail the random-walk test, and their predictability is profit only on paper.

title: Fat tails
bridge: Efficient markets looked at the direction of daily moves. Fat tails looks at their size, and at how often the US market has days that a normal distribution says should never happen.
blurb: In a century of US daily returns, 101 days moved more than five standard deviations, where a normal distribution expects one every 6,600 years. The tails fall like a power law with an exponent near 3, so a sample's kurtosis mostly records its worst day.

title: Value at risk
bridge: Fat tails showed how often big losses come. Value at risk turns the whole range of losses into one number for a bank's board, and this article shows what that number can miss.
blurb: One bond with a 4% chance of default has a 95% value at risk of zero, and $50 in each of two has one of $30. Value at risk reads one point of the loss curve, so spreading money can raise it, while expected shortfall averages the tail and falls.

title: Volatility clustering
bridge: Value at risk needs a forecast of how large losses can be. Volatility clustering shows that the size of daily moves has a memory, and builds the simplest forecast from it.
blurb: The sign of a daily move in US stocks is almost unpredictable and its size is not. A GARCH forecast with a half-life of about three months turns 1987 from a 16 standard deviation day into an 8.5 one, and leaves part of the fat tails unexplained.

title: Backtesting VaR
bridge: Volatility clustering built a forecast of tomorrow's risk. Backtesting VaR asks how a bank finds out whether such a forecast is any good, and why counting the days it was beaten says so little.
blurb: A year of 99% VaR exceptions is a count of about 2.5 rare days, so a model that's twice too optimistic is still green in 44% of years. On a century of US days, a model with exactly the right count was red in 8 of its 104 trading years.

title: Drawdowns
bridge: Backtesting VaR asked whether a risk model's bad days come as often as promised. Drawdowns looks at a strategy's worst fall from a peak, and why it keeps getting deeper the longer we watch.
blurb: A strategy's worst drawdown grows with the length of its record: like the square root of time with no edge, and like its logarithm with one. So live trading goes past a backtest's worst half the time within the backtest's own length, even when nothing has changed.

title: Bond prices and yields
bridge: Drawdowns closed the stage on market risk. Bond prices and yields starts on fixed income, with the one rate that prices all of a bond's payments and what it does and doesn't promise.
blurb: At an unchanged yield every bond earns its yield, whatever its coupon. Held to maturity, though, a bond earns its yield on only a share of its life, its average wait over its maturity, so a 30-year 8% bond earns 5.84% when rates fall to 4%.

title: Duration and convexity
bridge: Bond prices and yields found two forces pulling on a bondholder's money when rates move. Duration and convexity finds the horizon where they cancel, and why that leaves a small gain rather than nothing.
blurb: Duration is a bond's average wait, the slope of its price and the one horizon at which a parallel move in rates can't leave us short of the promised return. Convexity turns that floor into a small gain, which is why markets charge for it.

title: The yield curve and forward rates
bridge: Duration and convexity treated every maturity as having the same rate. The yield curve and forward rates gives each maturity its own, and asks what the forward rates locked in by those prices really tell us.
blurb: Bootstrapping turns coupon bond prices into spot rates one maturity at a time, and forward rates are the break-evens they lock in. Even when investors expect rates to stay put and ask nothing for risk, convexity pulls long forward rates below the expected rate.

title: The Merton model
bridge: The yield curve and forward rates priced loans that are sure to be repaid. The Merton model turns to loans that might not be, and reads a firm's chance of default off the price of its shares.
blurb: A firm's shares are a call option on its assets, so their price and how much they move pin down what the assets are worth and how risky they are. The chance of default that comes out is the market's, which overstates the real chance most for the safest firms.

title: The credit spread puzzle
bridge: The Merton model found that a share price implies the market's chance of default, not the real one. The credit spread puzzle compares a century of corporate bond yields with the defaults that really happened.
blurb: Since 1919, Moody's Baa bonds have yielded 1.16 points a year more than Aaa bonds, several times what their defaults cost. Paying lenders for when defaults happen explains most of the gap, and a 32-year record of defaults is far less certain than it looks.

title: Forwards and futures
bridge: The credit spread puzzle ended the stage on bonds. Forwards and futures starts on derivatives, with the price for delivering something later, and why it isn't anyone's forecast.
blurb: A forward price is the cost of buying now and carrying to delivery, pinned by an arbitrage whatever anyone expects. For oil, which can be stored but not lent, that's only a ceiling, which is how oil for May 2020 cost minus $37.63.

title: Put–call parity
bridge: Forwards and futures priced a promise to buy later. Put–call parity builds the same promise from a call and a put, and reads the forward the market is using off option prices.
blurb: A call minus a put is a forward in any model, so two models that disagree about every option agree on the difference. Run backwards, parity shows what a share costs to borrow: in March 2000, Palm's options priced its shares 23% to 29% below their price.

title: Binomial option pricing
bridge: Put–call parity priced the difference between a call and a put without a model. Binomial option pricing prices a single call on a tree, by copying it with shares and a loan.
blurb: When a share can only go up or down, a call can be copied, so its price doesn't depend on the real chance of a rise, though its expected return does. Many steps converge to Black and Scholes, and a third branch brings the real chances back.

title: Time diversification
bridge: Binomial option pricing priced a single option by copying it. Time diversification asks what happens to the risk of stocks as we hold them for longer, and why lower odds of losing aren't the same as smaller losses.
blurb: Holding stocks for longer lowers the chance that they end behind bonds, from 42% over one year to 14% over thirty. But the average shortfall when they do grows from 13% to 37%, and a 1-in-20 bad outcome keeps getting worse for 17 years.

title: Samuelson’s fallacy of large numbers
bridge: Time diversification showed that holding for longer lowers the odds of a shortfall and deepens it. Samuelson's 1963 paper asks whether repeating a bet we'd refuse once can ever make it worth taking.
blurb: If we'd refuse a bet at every level of wealth we could reach, we should refuse a hundred of them too. For someone with constant risk aversion, a hundred bets are worth a hundred times one, so the answer never flips.

title: Bodie’s shortfall insurance
bridge: Samuelson argued that repeating a risk doesn't shrink it. Bodie's 1995 paper puts a price on long-run risk by asking what it costs to insure stocks against ending behind bonds.
blurb: Insuring stocks against ending behind bonds costs about 8% of the money for one year and 42% for thirty, even as the chance of needing it falls. The price depends only on volatility and time, never on the premium stocks are expected to earn.

title: Isolation Forest
blurb: Anomalies are few, and they are different. Both of those make them easy to cut off from everything else — and that is the whole algorithm.

title: XGBoost
blurb: Why predict the answer when you can predict your own mistakes? How trees, gradients and shrinkage turn a sequence of simple rules into the default model for tabular data.

title: LightGBM
blurb: Bucket a column into 255 bins and the search for its best split stops being a scan over rows. It costs less than half a percent of the accuracy — and the speed does not come from where almost everyone says it does.

title: K-Means
blurb: Two moves, repeated until nothing changes. The algorithm always stops, it never makes things worse, and it is under no obligation whatsoever to be right.

title: Autoencoders
blurb: Squeeze data through a narrow layer and ask for it back, and a linear autoencoder rediscovers principal component analysis — in a basis nobody asked for, which it will never fix, because nothing in the loss can tell the difference.

title: Shapley Values
blurb: Three people, one fee, and no obvious way to split it. The answer game theory settled in 1953 turns out to be the answer to a question nobody was asking then: what did each feature contribute to this prediction?

title: SMOTE
blurb: The whole algorithm is one line: put a new minority point somewhere on the segment between two old ones. That line is a claim about the space between — where the claim is false, and what it was buying you anyway.

title: F1 Score
blurb: Maximising F1 on a validation set is the standard way to pick a classification threshold. The rule has a closed form, it is not about your problem, and it asserts a cost ratio nobody chose.

title: DBSCAN & HDBSCAN
blurb: Every value of eps you could try is one horizontal line drawn across the same tree. When the branches do not line up, none of them is right — not a hard search, an empty set — and HDBSCAN's answer is to stop cutting straight.

title: Population Stability Index
blurb: Every reading is how far the population moved plus (B−1)(1/N + 1/M), and the second term is there whether anything moved or not. The 0.10 and 0.25 lines ignore it — so on a small segment the traffic light is mostly reporting your sample size, and on a large one it cannot see a shift worth eight points of approval rate.

title: Peer groups and outliers
blurb: A field guide to k-means as a transaction-monitoring detector, tested on one synthetic bank from the raw data to the reason given to an investigator. K-means spends a centroid wherever it removes the most inertia, so a mule ring of 40 is flagged about a quarter as often as a lone mule, and the transform, the cap, the scaler and even who is in the table decide which typologies can be seen at all.

title: Pástor and Stambaugh’s long-run volatility
bridge: Bodie priced long-run risk with the premium left out. Pástor and Stambaugh's 2012 paper asks how volatile stocks look over long horizons once we admit we don't know the premium, or much else.
blurb: With a century of data, not knowing the mean adds 30% to the variance per year of a thirty-year forecast. Add doubt about how long expected returns persist, and the long run can look riskier per year than a single year, even with mean reversion.

title: Stocks for the long run in 39 markets
bridge: Pástor and Stambaugh asked what an investor can't know. Anarkulova, Cederburg and O'Doherty ask what the US record can't show, by pooling 39 developed markets.
blurb: In a world of 39 identical markets, the luckiest record puts the chance of a thirty-year real loss at about 1.7% when the truth is 13.7%. Luck in its growth rate shifts the odds by about one standard deviation at thirty years.

title: The Merton share
bridge: With the risks of the long run laid out, we turn to how much stock to hold at all. The Merton share is the one-line answer the rest of the section builds on.
blurb: Hold the premium over the variance, scaled down by risk aversion: 77% with a 5-point premium, 18% volatility and a risk aversion of 2. The top is flat, but a premium estimated from a century of data gives away 13% of the gain, and thirteen years gives it all away.

title: Samuelson and Merton’s lifetime portfolio
bridge: The Merton share is a one-year answer. Samuelson's and Merton's 1969 papers solve a whole lifetime of choices backwards to see whether the horizon changes it.
blurb: Solved backwards from the last year, the best share in stocks is 84% at every horizon and every level of wealth in our coin-flip market. A floor to stay above, or returns that revert, bring the horizon back.

title: Human capital
bridge: Samuelson and Merton's investor had only savings. A young worker also owns decades of future pay, and counting it as wealth changes the answer more than anything else.
blurb: Counting future pay as a bond, Merton's rule asks a 25-year-old for about 43 times her savings in stocks. The share falls below 100% only around 62, so any borrowing limit binds for decades, unless her pay moves with the market.

title: Bodie, Merton and Samuelson’s flexible worker
bridge: The human capital article counted a worker's future pay as wealth. Bodie, Merton and Samuelson's 1992 paper asks what changes when she can also choose how many hours to work.
blurb: A worker who can trade hours for pay after a loss holds more stock at the same wealth, 1.5 times as much at a risk aversion of 2. The factor is the same at every level of savings and every number of years left.

title: Cocco, Gomes and Maenhout’s life-cycle portfolio
bridge: Bodie, Merton and Samuelson let a worker choose her hours. Cocco, Gomes and Maenhout's 2005 paper fixes them, makes her pay risky and adds a rule against borrowing.
blurb: With no borrowing, a worker of moderate risk aversion holds all stocks for decades, and a limit of 2 to 1 only postpones the day it stops binding. Being unable to borrow costs 3.0% of consumption every year at a risk aversion of 3, and 0.16% at 10.

title: Benzoni, Collin-Dufresne and Goldstein’s cointegrated pay
bridge: Cocco, Gomes and Maenhout tied pay to stocks with a fixed correlation. Benzoni, Collin-Dufresne and Goldstein's 2007 paper lets pay follow dividends over the long run, and that treats young and old workers differently.
blurb: If pay follows dividends with a lag, far-off paydays behave like stock and near ones like a bond. With a half-life of 5 years, the rule asks a 25-year-old for a small short position, and half a year more turns it into 98%.

title: Lifecycle leverage
bridge: The last three articles kept running into a limit on borrowing. Lifecycle leverage asks what borrowing would do for a saver who adds a little each year, and where it would help.
blurb: A saver's market risk is lumpier than it is lopsided: the last ten years carry a third of the exposure. Borrowing 2 to 1 early, at the same total exposure, narrows the spread of final wealth by 8% and costs 2% of the median.

title: The cost of leverage
bridge: Lifecycle leverage borrowed at the safe rate, which nobody can do. The cost of leverage puts a spread on the loan and asks how much of the plan is left.
blurb: A loan that costs 2 points more than the safe rate splits Merton's rule at 100%, and savers with a risk aversion between 0.93 and 1.54 hold exactly 100%. It also takes a young saver's leverage from 4,299% of savings to 1,879%.
